label: Claude Haiku 5.5
output:
# Fourteen Years of Nights

I did my last night shift on Saturday. Nine till half seven, majors, the usual mix of chest pains, falls, a drunk man who was very sorry, and a child with a bead up her nose who was not sorry at all. I handed over at 07:30, walked out into the car park, and didn't feel much of anything. I was tired, which is normal. I had been tired for fourteen years, which is not.

From Monday I'm on days only. My knees have had enough of the stairs and the sudden drops in energy at four in the morning. My sleep has never recovered from being pushed around the clock. And my GP has finally stopped treating my blood pressure as a joke. It was the right decision. I've been saying so to everyone, and I believe it, and I'm still not okay about it.

I started nights in 2012 as an SHO, twenty-eight years old and sure I could handle anything. I could, mostly, but nights taught me that handling it and being fine about it are different things.

The first winter, I cried in the car park at the Infirmary. I'd done a shift that was busy but not terrible, and somewhere around half three I had been standing at the drug trolley trying to remember whether I had given a patient their second dose. I couldn't picture it. I went out to my car, sat there with the engine off, and cried in a way I hadn't since I was a kid. When I finally looked up, the windscreen was white with frost, and I remember thinking the frost looked like someone had drawn on it from the inside. I went back in and checked the chart. I had given it. I'd known I had, and I still needed to check. That is what nights do to you in the first year. They make you doubt the things you're surest of, and then they make you do the job anyway.

Last winter, around three in the morning, an old gentleman in a bay by the far wall reached out and took my hand while I was doing his obs. He didn't say anything for a while. Then he told me I had his daughter's hands. I didn't ask him about her and he didn't say more. He went home three days later. I think about him more than I'd have expected, usually when I'm washing my hands, which I suppose is what that moment was about.

I want to be honest about what nights gave me, because it's easy to make the whole thing sound like a hardship, and it wasn't only that.

Nights are where the department is most itself. During the day there are more managers, more meetings, more people asking how things are going, and more people who have to be seen to be doing something. At night there are fewer of them. What's left is the people doing the work, and they're much more honest. You can say "I don't think this man is going home" at four in the morning and be listened to. You can say "I'm not sure" and nobody performs confidence at you. There's a kind of plain decency in the small hours that I haven't found anywhere else in medicine.

People assume nights run on adrenaline. Some of it does. But most of it, if I'm honest, is about staying kind when you are completely empty. It's about speaking to a confused man for the fifth time in an hour as if it's the first. It's about remembering that the woman in cubicle six has been waiting since eleven and is frightened, even if she's being rude about it. Kindness at five in the morning costs more than it does at noon, and most nights I paid it without thinking. I'm not sure I'll be able to put that down easily.

Nights also cost me things I can list. I missed both my nieces' naming ceremonies. I watched one of them on a video call, propped on the kitchen counter, half asleep, while my sister held the baby up to the camera and said, "Say hello to Uncle Aidan." My sister has never once complained about this. Not once. I've found that harder to forgive myself for than anything the rota did.

And then there's the drive home. Sunday morning, after the Saturday night, I came down the London Road with the sun coming up low and orange. The radio was on catch-up, and I'd put on the shipping forecast without thinking, because it's what you listen to after a shift like that. Viking, North Utsire, South Utsire. The sun was in the mirror and the road was empty and I realised I would not see that particular light from this side again. I had to pull over for a minute. Not because of anything dramatic. Just because it was the last time it would be mine in that way.

I'm relieved. That's the part I keep stumbling over. I'm relieved to be going, and I feel like a traitor for being relieved, as if fourteen years of nights should have earned me the right to be devastated instead of simply tired and grateful. I've decided to stop arguing with the feeling. It's allowed to be two things.

This isn't a complaint about staffing. I've written enough of those, and they were true, and they didn't change anything I needed changing. It's just a record of what I'm leaving.

What I'll take with me, I think, is Folasade. She's been charge nurse on nights for twenty-two years. She knows where everything is, who's going to be trouble, and which registrar will need a sit-down before he admits he needs one. On Saturday, when we went up the back stairs to the ward at the end of the shift because the lift was out again, she was ahead of me the whole way, not even breathing hard. She didn't look back. At the top she said, "Your knees going, then?" and I said yes, and she said, "Mm," in the particular tone she uses for things she's already decided are your own fault. Then she held the door open for me.

And there's the toast. Someone always makes toast in the staff room at four in the morning. Nobody has ever admitted to starting it. It's been going on since before I arrived and I'm fairly sure it will go on after I've left, a small ritual that no one organised and everyone keeps. On Saturday, at four, the smell of it drifted down the corridor, and I stood in the doorway for a moment with my coat already on. Somebody had put a plate out. Nobody said anything. I took a piece, ate it standing up, and left it at that.

I won't be on nights any more, but I'll still be in the department. I'll still see the toast and the people who make it. And I'll be able to go home at six in the evening and sleep through the night like a normal person, which is a strange thing to look forward to after fourteen years. My knees will thank me. So, in a quieter way, will my sister, and my blood pressure, and probably Folasade, who will no longer have to wait for me on the stairs.

I'm still not okay about it. But I think I can be not okay and glad at the same time, which is more or less what nights taught me to do.
